summary:
**ORBITAL: Beyond the Impossible**

ORBITAL is an interactive 3D space mission simulator that turns anyone into a mission engineer. Players choose from five missions, from Earth observation to the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt and Jupiter. They then design a spacecraft from 12 components, including chemical and ion engines, fuel tanks, solar panels, RTGs, antennas and science instruments, and pick one of three rockets with real payload limits.

Every decision follows real physics: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, specific impulse, and sunlight that weakens with distance squared. During flight, players manage fuel, power and science data while responding to events like solar flares, micrometeorites, debris and communication failures. An in-game Mission Director explains each choice, so players learn by doing.

By building on NASA's open science and space-based data and technology (planetary orbits, ion propulsion, Voyager and Curiosity-style RTG power, and radiation and heliophysics data), ORBITAL makes complex mission trade-offs accessible, engaging and fun.

**Fail safely. Learn deeply. Try again.**
details:
The player picks one of five missions (Earth Observation, Lunar Landing, Mars Rover, Asteroid Survey, Jupiter Deep Space), then builds a spacecraft in a 3D workshop from 12 components: engines, fuel tanks, solar panels, batteries, antennas, science instruments, radiation shielding and landing legs. The 3D model changes as parts are added or removed, and the engineering numbers update at once: mass, cost, power, delta-v (from the rocket equation) and payload margin. The player then chooses a launch vehicle, and the game checks whether it can carry the craft. After a countdown and launch, the player flies the mission with pause and fast-forward controls and a live telemetry panel. Random emergencies appear (solar flares, debris, power loss, communication failure, fuel leaks). Each has three response options with real consequences that depend on the earlier design. A black-box timeline at the end explains what caused success or failure.

Benefits and intended impact: The game teaches how real missions are designed through play instead of a textbook. Players learn about trade-offs between mass, power and cost, why sunlight weakens with distance, why rockets have payload limits and why reserves matter. Short explanations appear as parts are chosen, and a Mission Director assistant answers questions like “Why is my power low?” The goal is to build interest in STEM and aerospace among students and curious players.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Three.js library (WebGL) for 3D graphics. All models, planets, particle effects and the interface are generated in code, so no paid assets or external services are needed. It runs on an ordinary PC in a standard browser, saves progress in local storage and is hosted with Git (GitHub Pages). Claude (by Anthropic) assisted with writing the code.

Creativity: It is a playable game rather than a quiz or dashboard. The same physics calculation (delta-v) drives both the design screen and the mission outcome. Emergencies depend on the player’s design, for example a ship with no shielding gets more solar flares.

Factors considered: Educational accuracy versus playability (physics is simplified and distances are scaled down), meaningful choices where nothing is free, accessibility with no install and plain-language explanations, and easy expansion because the parts, rockets and missions are simple data lists. It is a working vertical slice, and planned next steps include crew and life support, a what-if design lab, audio and planet textures.
